speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, September 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, be now read a second time and referred to a Legislative Committee, and the amendment of Mr. Frith (page 6625).

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the various Members speaking for the Opposition, as they commented on the amendment to the Bill now before the House.
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I express my support for this legislation which was introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and is aimed above all, and I think it is important to emphasize that this morning, at restructuring social benefit programs for Canadian families.
Mr. Speaker, by introducing this legislation, the Government has shown it takes its responsibilities seriously by providing a long-term perspective for our social programs, for the greater benefit of Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I always find it rather surprising that the same Opposition Members who have been very vociferous in this debate on social programs were on the Government benches for 20 years, during which they increased this country's debt in a way that was absolutely outrageous, without any consideration for the future and future generations. That we must not forget. Opposition Members keep telling us that enough has been said about the past and that all that is history. I disagree. We are going to talk about the past and they may be sure we will go on talking about it for some time.
During the debate last June on partial de-indexation of pensions, a number of Opposition Members were most inconsistent in their reactions, when they grossly exaggerated the impact of a sound and legitimate program that was presented to Canadian citizens, and in doing so, they completely distorted the debate and destroyed any hope of considering the issue in an objective and realistic manner.
Mr. Speaker, strangely enough, those very same Members who were previously on the Government side took the liberty of capping indexation of family allowances during the last ten years they were in power. If indexation had been maintained over the years, the family allowance would be $20 more than it is now. They never mention that. There are some things they would rather forget. We will get back to that later. The same people who prevented this $20 increase are complaining today about a reduction worth all of 94 cents. They are dramatizing and making a terrific fuss. The same people ... Mr. Speaker, I think I should repeat that it is easier for them to see the mote in their neighbour's eye than the beam in their own. That is quite obvious today.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: We cannot see you behind your beam!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
There are a lot of beams over there. There are quite a few, and we are going to try and remove them one by one. That will teach them to open their eyes, to see not just what suits them but also what does not. We are going to throw some light on the social and economic state of affairs here in Canada. Canadian citizens ought to know what really happened in the past and what is happening now in Canada.
If we could have had full indexation during the last ten years, perhaps that would have been a lesser evil. However, those same Liberal politicians governed this country so badly that we are now practically mired in debt, and today, they are talking about... I am thinking of one term, for instance, that has been quoted repeatedly in recent months. I am referring to the term universality. We had to maintain universality. Universality of what, may I ask, Mr. Speaker? The kind of universality we inherited from the previous government meant that all the provinces were opposed to the federal Government. Universality meant the deficit that affected every Canadian citizen. There was the universal concern among all Canadians and all this lasted until we were able to replace that government and Canadians told them loud and clear, in no uncertain terms, what they thought of their Government and the 20 years it was in power before we took over last September.
The Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) said yesterday, and I listened carefully to each and every speaker, that we were a Government of promises. Yes, that is true. We promised to establish a new climate of confidence in this country. And we have. Let them stop their false alarms and the panic button techniques they have been using during the past few

September 17, 1985

months. The people we all meet every weekend are not as upset and concerned as the Opposition would have us believe. We promised to re-establish an open and sincere dialogue with the provinces and to settle a host of problems that were pending and that had started to fester because of the arrogant attitude of the Government at the time.
[DOT] (mo)
We also promised to assume our responsibilities and come to grips with the suffocating deficit left us by the previous deserted-not to say routed-Government. In less than a year we managed to bring interest rates back to the lowest level in eight years, an inflation rate of barely 4 per cent whereas they kept it at 12 per cent for years.
An Elon. Member: Keep a straight face when you say that!

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
They conveniently forget those years, Mr. Speaker, and now that inflation stands at less than 4 per cent Canadians are looking to the future with confidence, especially with respect to the social affairs sector with which we are concerned today. Like most of my Government colleagues I have been visiting my riding every weekend for the last year. It gives us an opportunity to meet with youths, middle-aged people and heads of families who all have one thing in common, namely their concern about the future, the future of our country, the future of our youths. Simply to score political points, Mr. Speaker, no one has the right to upset everything and confuse people here in Canada while forgetting our future and that of our children. In fact the central issue of this debate today is our future. The Government of the day must face up to its responsibilities to ensure that elderly Canadians, our families and our youths do have a secure future. There is one thing those young people do not understand and they never fail to mention it to me: How could we possibly have been so blind, how is it that the previous Government was so inconsistent and irresponsible in the many decision it took over the years without even realizing or knowing where it was leading us? The one thing they do understand is that we are spending $25 billion a year simply to pay interests on the orgy of expenditures of the Members opposite over *the last twenty years. That is as much money as we spend on social affairs in Canada. They often get a chuckle out of the fact that additional taxes will have to be levied on corporate income, for this has already been announced in the Budget; a minimum tax will be imposed on high incomes. They know that, and so they should in my opinion. But we are responsible people, we have taken over and we will try to solve the problem. Our Government is steering a new course, Mr. Speaker, for we want to set some order in Government interventions in all endeavours, be they in the economic or social sector. Business circles and high income individuals-and this is one of our commitments which is sometimes not taken seriously-will have to do their share through additional corporate taxes already announced in the Budget. They know a minimum tax will be payable on high incomes, and I should think that Opposition Members of the
New Democratic Party ought to be particularly pleased about that, considering they have been asking for that since God knows when. Here we are responding favourably to one of their requests, yet they are not delighted. Come on now! What will they talk about? What will they beef about next? That, Mr. Speaker, is reality, those are facts and they ought to be honest enough to admit it.
Notwithstanding what the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) may have said yesterday, our American friends and neighbours are quite worried about their soaring expenditures and the ever worsening deficit problem. Mr. Speaker, the coming months and years will prove that the Canadian Government showed the way to the western world by coming to grips with its deficit and attempting to find a long term solution to this problem. As much in Sudbury as anywhere else, Canadians are fully aware of the fact that our Government has taken very little time to put 300,000 people back to work by creating new jobs in co-operation with the private sector which has regained full confidence in the economy and the Government. Indeed what we have restored among Canadians is much more a matter of attitude, of mentality, of confidence. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to set our social policy on the right track, because the previous Government did not know where it was heading and could only come up with band-aid and haphazard policies. They could not see very far into the future. That is what we did by revamping the whole sector.
Yesterday the Hon. Member for Sudbury said something about hypocrisy, yet the people in his own Government were the ones who stood in the way of full indexation of family allowances, with the result that the recipients are now deprived of $20. They are getting $20 less than they would have had it been maintained. Certainly he has forgotten all about that. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) has no recollection of it, he was not here. It is my understanding he was living in other climates. I do not know whether those were more favourable climates, but I have some doubts. Had he been happy, maybe he would not have looked for a change.

Turning to the Hon. I remembered that when I saw his candid face in the papers, recently. His picture was in the press in 1975, when he was Minister of Finance and universality was not that important. Now he stands up in this House, banging on his desk, and insisting he will fight for the universality of social programs, and any change will have to be made over his dead body. When our friends opposite refer to maintaining the same social benefits for families, they no doubt forget that the major social benefit that does or should exist in our society is having a job. We believe that people would rather have a job. My colleague for Laval-des-Rapides estimated that in 1990, people with income in the $10,000 to $20,000 range will have lost approximately 4 per cent. But we as a Government want people in 1990 to have jobs, we want people to be back at work rather than to sit down waiting for social benefits to come. What Canadians want is employment. People will then be assessing our approach to social measures using standards other than social benefits for the unemployed.
As I often say, Mr. Speaker, there are people who sometimes fight over assumptions. There is a guy who used to live not far from my home. He used to say: I would rather have 5 per cent of something than 50 per cent of nothing. We sometimes suspect, when Opposition members discuss or advocate positions, that what they are proposing are measures they "forsee" and not too clearly at that. Mr. Speaker, that is what our Government is working at. There are none so deaf as those who do not want to hear. And for weeks we have seen the Liberal members opposite shed crocodile tears. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) mentioned the quality of life of women at home. Mr. Speaker, I caution the Hon. Members opposite. If they intend to get on a horse and act like Don Quixote and travel around the country trying to smash down windmills, they can be sure that we will not let them do so. We will take the necessary steps to explain clearly the information circulated on that legislation and make sure that the opposition will not launch a witch hunt. You can be sure of that.
When the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) rose yesterday, he was uneasy at the beginning and wasted 10 minutes before he started to say something. His Government agreed that it was wrong to deindex old age pensions. Senior citizens and their supporters across the country said it was wrong because it was eroding universal old age pensions. Mr. Speaker, to continue the debate on this subject, the main issue is that this Government has decided to de-index the value of family allowances down to 3 per cent each year, starting in 1986. This means that in 1986, they are going to take 94 cents or a dollar

September 17, 1985
Family Allowances Act
away from the children of poor families, per month, and then $2 and $3 and $4 and so on.
In fact, the Progressive Conservative Government has decided to continue the policies of the Liberal Government. This means that it does not respect the principle of universality on which the family allowance program was based and has been for 40 years.
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat familiar with these problems because in the forties, my father, as an adviser to the Government, was involved in setting up the welfare programs after World War II. The House will recall it was a Liberal Government at the time that was apprehensive about the people's support for the CCF, the predecessor of the New Democratic Party, because we on our side were pushing for the establishment of a social security program that would cover everyone. We wanted a program that would be universal and cover all Canadians, and not just those who were in greatest need, because we knew from the Depression, that means tests were not satisfactory, tended to set people against each other, and practically guaranteed that social security programs would not be adequate for those who were living in poverty.
Mr. Speaker, since that time and for many years we have maintained the principle of universality, but as the Minister said yesterday in his introduction to the debate, during the last ten years, the cuts imposed by the Liberal Government have had the effect of reducing family allowances by $20 a month. At the beginning of the 70s, family allowances were worth about $20 per child, and now, with full indexation, the program could have been worth about $51 per month today. It was not the Conservatives but the Liberals who imposed reductions, cuts and de-indexation. More recently, it was the 6 and 5 program that reduced the monthly value of family allowances by about 10 per cent. In 1979, they reduced the increase in value of family allowances from 11 per cent to zero. The Liberals created a precedent, and now the Conservative Government is following suit. Now it is not just for one or two years. They intend to make it permanent. Some vague promises have been made about what could be done in the future, but basically, it is clear that the Conservative Government is very sympathetic to a further reduction in the value of family allowances and of all kinds of benefits aimed at the families of this country.
Mr. Speaker, after what was said by the Member who spoke previously, I wonder how he could possibly ... he referred to Santa Claus. He said that we, the New Democratic Party, believed in Santa Claus. I do believe in Santa Claus, and I hope he does too, because this is very important to children. I wonder how in the present situation, we could possibly mistake the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for the Government's Santa Claus. So Santa Claus has now become very strict; he feels he has to take nickels and dimes from small kids, particularly those from poor families, he takes money away from them!
Now then, I do not know whether he is aware of what the rest of the Government is doing, but if we consider the budgetary policy of the Government, what with deindexation of family allowances as announced in the Budget, we can see that rich people, those who have clout, the very small percentage of people who make capital gains, we can see that those are the very people who receive from the same Government that takes food away from small children.
And then we have the Government's own Mrs. Santa Claus-the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) from Toronto-who is just as severe as Santa Claus, who also takes small change from kids and then turns around and hands out billions of dollars to companies, institutions and banks which had deposits in the Canadian Commercial Bank.
So here we are wondering how could that Minister, Mrs. Santa Claus, hand out $1 billion to bankers over a weekend while at the same time the Minister of National Health and Welfare takes money away from children, $103 million a year for starters and all the way up to $600 million a year by 1990.
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw your attention to the fact that the Government is trying to convince us that it has to take money away from children to balance the books. Yet at the same time it gives money to bankers, quite oblivious to its own argument that bank presidents should not really get family allowances because they can do without them. 1 should think they do not need any money, they just got $1 billion from the Minister of State (Finance). The Government gives with one hand and takes with the other, but it takes from the poor, from low income families and gives it all to the rich.

I should like to draw to the attention of the House some of the figures in terms of poverty among families, the purpose of a universal program of family allowances, the very real dangers in the dismantling of unversality under the Government and the disparity which occurs when a Government is prepared to give $1 billion to bankers in one weekend at the same time as it is prepared to take away $130 million this coming year and up to $600 million in 1990 from the mouths of children and of families, most often families with very modest incomes.
The National Council on Welfare has made a very serious study on the impact of the 1985 Budget on families at different levels of income. It has cumulated the impact over the course of the next five years, until 1990. No matter how we compare it, families with low incomes and children consistently lose more than families with high incomes and children. The middle class gets hit, too. I think what is most unconscionable is the fact that if you consider a family earning $80,000, because of the increase in the Budget in the exemption for Registered Retirement Savings Plans, because of the fact that capital gains up to $500,000 are now going to be totally exempt from tax, the $80,000 a year family comes out much better off, relatively speaking, than the $15,000 a year family.

Let us look at the figures. In 1990 the total loss, because of the Budget, to a family earning $15,000 a year will be $1,879. The total loss to the $80,000 a year family will be $1,125.
That is really progressive fiscal policy. You take more from the people who have low incomes, perhaps because there are so many of them, and you take less from people earning $80,000 a year who surely in our society are able to make a larger rather than a smaller contribution.
Mr. Speaker, consider a one-earner couple with two children and compare family earnings. Believe me, where people can afford to have one income it is usually a very big income, but the loss to a one-earner family with an income is $15,000 a year is going to be $2,422 by 1990. The extremely modest and brief increase in the total child package in 1986 and 1987 will be nowhere near enough to compensate for the other tax losses that that family will suffer. So they lose $2,422.
In the name of tax equity, what has the Government done for the family with one earner earning $80,000 a year? They are obviously so badly off that they need to be looked after. And they will come out, after five years, Mr. Speaker, $5,622 ahead. They in fact get lower taxes over the next five years, while the family who is trying to scrape by on $15,000 a year loses the equivalent of $500 a year over the next five years.
Last night I was knocking on some doors in my riding of Ottawa Centre. I talked to a number of people and said; "What is on your mind?" They said to me: "The family allowance, it just ain't fair." They said to me: "Look, it was not fair to deindex the old age pension for senior citizens and no more is it fair to deindex the family allowance for families."
I think they understood something which the Hon. Members on the government side do not understand and that is the reason we brought in family allowances originally and the reasons as well why we in our Party have always advocated that this be a universal program rather than a program which is only directed to people on very modest incomes.
One of the reasons why it is a universal program is, very simply, this. If you take two families, one with a couple of kids and the other childless, and their income is the same, I do not think that it takes a lot of reflection to realize that it costs more to pay the living expenses of the family with kids. Kids eat. They require bedrooms, a place to sleep, clothing, more housing is required. It costs money to go to the dentist; we don't have dental care in most parts of Canada. They need toys and entertainment. It costs money to take them to McDonald's or places like that.

So someone who works a lifetime, as some of the people in my riding do, to earn half a million dollars and is taxed year after year is going to be paying for Parliament, paying for defence, paying for social programs, paying for economic programs, not just for himself or herself, but on behalf of the coupon-clipper who is making half a million dollars of capital gains and is not having to pay any tax at all.
I would suggest that it is about time we started to look at things in that perspective rather than try to whip up into a frenzy that kind of welfare bum psychology where people say it is wrong to be giving social spending payments or to be redistributing income to people because they are poor, because they are raising children, because they are old and have contributed to our society over the course of their productive lifetime.

Speaker, when he got up in the House of Commons and said that all kinds of groups were telling him that they have to do this in order to make their contribution to the deficit. 1 was one, Mr. Speaker, who said, "Name one group of senior citizens who support the deindexation proposals". Put in specific terms, that 94 cents means one litre of

milk being taken away from each kid in 1986 per month, two litres in 1987, three litres in 1988 and a litre per week in 1990. That is what is being taken away.
What is being done on the other side? I mentioned some figures with respect to the amounts coming into the hands of families who are rich. That seems to me to be totally and entirely perverse.
I wish to remind Hon. Members of the fact that under the Liberal administration over the course of the last 30 or 40 years, despite the occasionally constructive efforts the Liberals made to redistribute income, the distribution of income in our society remains as unjust today as it was in 1945 or 1950. The bottom 20 per cent of families, in terms of incomes, receive 6 per cent of incomes, while the top 20 per cent of families in our society receive 40 per cent of incomes. Thus, the families at the top are receiving six or seven times the amount of real resources per annum as compared to the families at the bottom. The Conservative Government's response to that situation has been to implement the capital gains exemption and other measures which place more resources into the pockets of those families at the top while taking them away from families at the bottom.
Finally, I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, and my hon. colleagues opposite, that the defence put forward by the Government which is to say, "We have put money in the pockets of people with low incomes", is totally specious. Mr. Speaker, inshore fishermen on the East Coast are battling the Conservative bureaucracy once again. The herring fishery closed in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island last week because the quota was caught. Knowing the waters are teeming with herring, the fishermen asked for an increase in quota. The Minister said no to the New Brunswick fishermen. Prince Edward Island fishermen are still waiting for an answer.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand that answer. It comes at a time when the herring are schooling in the Northumberland Strait and the markets are strong. Herring is the toughest fishery at which to make a decent living. Why not let the fishermen catch the herring while they are in the waters? The herring will be gone within a week.
Increasing the quota would help the plant workers as well. They desperately need the jobs the extra quota would provide. Unemployment is a way of life in that area. The herring fishery on the East Coast is in a desperate situation, so desperate that New Brunswick fishermen are ignoring the closure. They have been fishing illegally since last weekend. I don't support them, but the Government is seizing the catches and selling them to the processors who are writing cheques to the Receiver General. What does the Government intend to do with the profit? Give it to the needy fishermen or use it to pay off the federal deficit? Why did the Minister not have the foresight to predict that this would happen? Where was he this summer when he should have been consulting with fishermen? What was he doing-fishing salmon in B.C.?
It is time for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) to listen to fishermen and to pay attention to their concerns. The Government promised to maintain the inshore fishery, but fishermen on the East Coast can see throught that promise.

SOUTH AFRICA-INVASION OF ANGOLA-CALL FOR MANDATORY SANCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday amid great fanfare the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) announced a series of largely voluntary sanctions purportedly designed to send a message to the South African Government that Canada wants a change in apartheid and in the status of Namibia. The leaders of blacks within South Africa, Namibia, and the front line states had asked for mandatory sanctions since they realized that volun-
September 17, 1985

tary sanctions were not enough. Once again they were proven right because today we have South Africa's answer to our gentle prodding. It has once again invaded Angola with the military might supplied by the West.
Yesterday's actions by South Africa should not be a surprise to the Canadian Government in light of the type of measures which were announced. These include a ban on air travel that does not exist, a voluntary ban on bank loans that are no longer being made, and a voluntary embargo on oil exports that are largely insignificant anyway.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs promised tougher sanctions if things did not improve. Clearly matters have worsened. It is time for tough economic sanctions and leadership in the Commonwealth.

THE LATE LIEUTENANT GENERAL E. L. M. BURNS TRIBUTE TO DISTINGUISHED CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay respect to a great Canadian who died on Friday, September 6.
Lieutenant General E. L. M. Burns, a distinguished soldier, engineer and diplomat, will long be remembered for his unselfish contribution to the Government of Canada.
General Burns graduated from the Royal Military College of Canada, was commissioned in the Royal Canadian Engineers in 1915 and won the Military Cross in World War I.
During peace time he experimented in the field of air photo surveys and served as president of the Canadian Institue of Surveying in 1936-1937.
General Burns commanded the first Canadian Corps during operations in the Liri Valley in 1944.
Following the Second World War he became involved in the movement toward peacekeeping and disarmament with the Department of External Affairs.
General Burns was loaned from the Department to the UN in 1954 and was appointed Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. In the ensuing years he played a role in the Suez crisis, the Sinai, and was named Special Adviser to the Government of Canada on Disarmament.
General Burns was awarded the Pearson Peace Medal in 1981 in recognition of this brave Canadian's dedication. On behalf of all men and women who believe personal sacrifice is the route to world peace. General Burns will be missed by all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the comments and accusations of the Opposition regarding the failure of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
As an Albertan, and as the Member for the constituency in which the bank operated, I cannot believe the Liberals could stand up in this House with a clear conscience and criticize us for attempting to help a fledgling financial institution which, in reality, failed due to the National Energy Program.
The Canadian Commercial Bank existed for western Canadians-of that I am proud. The bank, as well as many other institutions in the West, could never have foreseen the devastating effects of the NEP. The bank rose out of a growing economic infrastructure-until the Liberals chopped it down. Such a small institution could never protect itself against the National Energy Program, which was a steamroller of economic ruin in Alberta.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) have said if we allowed the bank to fail without making a valiant effort to save it? He probably would have said that the Government was forgetting about the West. Well, we did not forget about the West. It is simply hard to compete against the crushing policies of the previous Liberal Government.
We will not apologize for helping an Alberta institution. I am proud to say we did what we could. I am also proud to sit in the same Chamber as the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall).

speechtext:
I was following the course of this debate to this point with considerable interest and trying to examine for myself what was happening in the House and how the debate was proceeding. I was glad this morning that the Government side was not going to content itself with just the bald statements of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) in relation to the planned reduction of family allowances, both as a component of government spending and as a component of family budgets in Canada.
I was glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais) and the Member from Winnipeg South rising in what I took to be somewhat stage-managed efforts to defend the Government's position. It struck me in listening to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, along with speakers from this Party and from the Official Opposition, that what we were looking at was an excellent portrayal of the disparate motives within the Progressive Con-

September 17, 1985
Family Allowances Act
servative Party, undoubtedly around the Cabinet table and within the government caucus.
On the one hand we heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare defending the reduction of family allowance payments as being a marginal adjustment, something that did not compromise the principle of universality, something that was, in fact, a little tinkering with the works that was not going to have any effect at all on the budgets of ordinary Canadians. On the other hand, and by contrast, we had the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) expounding what 1 believe is a tradition within the Progressive Conservative Party that is not going to lie down, a tradition which says that social payments are some form of wastage in the economy, a tradition which decries and denigrates social payments as some form of charity. For example, there was a reference to $60 billion of social expenditures by the Government. This reference did not enable Members of this House, listeners or readers outside of this House to understand the relative significance in budgetary and national account terms. It was merely a reference to global figures, and, by implication, a reference to the generosity which this represented, presumably to the more productive classes of Canadians as opposed to those he sees as unproductive classes.
I would like to tell the Government and point out to the Progressive Conservative Party that until that sort of thinking is eliminated, there may be those Canadians who will elect them but they will be short of Canadians who will trust them.
It seems to me the Government was rightly nervous in allowing its Members to speak to this debate. Some credit is deserved. The Government has decided to grasp the nettle of what sentiments might come out from some of the wilder fringes of that caucus. On the one hand we have the preoccupation with the deficit, and there is legitimate concern with the deficit, and on the other hand we have an ideological viewpoint which views social expenditures as some form of subsidy, some form of scrap thrown to the poor people in order to buy their silence and their compliance.

subsubtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
As one who is occasionally guilty of the conduct complained of, I was not going to complain myself, Mr. Speaker. I do not doubt the Government side has very important matters it would like to resolve before Ministers escape to the relative safety of their ministerial offices. Of course I know, as a practising politician, that the practice of talking over one another is useful. However, when it reaches the ear of the Speaker it seems to be meaningless chatter, although I do not doubt the relevance and indeed the importance of what was being said.
I should like to return to the theme which has been taken up by speakers in this Party and in the Official Opposition. I would ask Government Members why they are not questioning the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), their Cabinet and their Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as to the status of the election promises which were made by the Progressive Conservative Party. Of course those election promises said nothing about reducing family allowances in the context of the over-all social spending envelope. Those promises, however, had much to say about maintaining indexation. To use an outworn phrase which will never leave the consciousness of Canadians, those promises had much to say about the sacred trust which our social programs imposed and should impose on every Member of the House.
The nature of the Bill is simply the adjustment of the family allowances. All Hon. Members, in speaking to it, have chosen to discuss it in a wider context. I have no hesitation in following that precedent. While we have heard from the Government side that apparently every evil which has afflicted the country over the past decade can be traced to the National Energy Program, we have also heard some contexts that are eminently sensible as an analysis of what the Government is trying to do with the family allowance reductions. It is worth pointing out in the House the removal of indexation in the sense that indexation is now to be dropped by three percentage points and that only the incremental inflation above 3 per cent will be counted in the recalculation of family allowances. Even though that form of indexation provides for an increase every year in the family allowance payments, it does not, in and of itself, give a share of the increase in Canada's wealth and Canada's means to the people who are the main beneficiaries of family allowances, namely, the poorest of the poor. Because indexation merely links an increase in payments to the value of money, it does not take into account increases in our Gross National Product. It does not take into account policy directions or the possibility that we, as Canadians, would like to see some of the increase in our national wealth also shared with people who are undertaking-and let us never forget that-a very serious responsibility not only on their own behalf but on behalf of all. There are those people who will benefit from the fact that the Government has not reintroduced the marginal tax rates which the previous Liberal Government discarded in a pay-off to its wealthier supporters. There are the people who will benefit from the lifetime capital gains bonanza or exemption. There are the people who will benefit from the removal of the limit on RRSP contributions, and the people who will undoubtedly benefit from the tax breaks which the Government will introduce in the future. They will be raising their children in the same society as those people who will be losing because of the Government's regressive behaviour in terms of family allowances.
One thing has always struck me about Canada since I came here 15 years ago. It did have and still has today strong elements of feeling about being one society. Canada is mercifully free of the classism and elitism of the society which I left
September 17, 1985

to come here. I believe that that organic picture of society to which we as Canadians largely, although not totally, subscribe by our actions is a philosophy, an impression and a credo that the Government should be doing everything to reinforce and nothing, in my opinion, to denigrate. With the family allowance being reduced and with the compensating increase for a period of only two years in the child tax credit, we should look at the message which those changes are sending to Canadians. We should look at the fact that over a 5-year span there will be no families which gain from the proposals of the Government. We should consider the message which is being sent to families, particularly poorer families, by those type of adjustments. We should consider the impression of Canadians when they are confronted with those calculations and understand that by the year 1990 all those who are parenting will be losers from this package of measures. They will very likely see, as I see, the measures introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare as being a niggardly tinkering with our social support network. We should consider what the reduced exemptions for children will do to the income tax system. We should consider the impression in the minds of the parents of Canada when they juxtapose the Government's reduction in the effective increase in the family allowance with a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that Canada has an acute shortage of rich people. We should consider what will be the impression of the average family when it realizes that the family allowance reduction will reduce its over-all budget and income.
Some Members of the House have spoken of the reduction in the increase in family allowances as an attack on families. To others that may sound like rhetoric. However, I believe that it contains a very important element of truth and significance. After all, it is never reality which governs the reactions, behaviour and beliefs of people in this country or in any other country; it is always the perception of what is happening. The Government is sending a clear message by these reductions to the people of Canada, particularly to the poorest families, that so far as it is concerned child rearing, parenting and the development and growth of families are less a concern this year than they were last year. They will be even less a concern in 1990 than they are this year, and they will be an ever-diminishing concern of the Government from now on.
We should also consider what will happen if the average Canadian family relates family allowance receipts to its budget and the cost of raising children. The family allowance, the child tax credit and the child tax exemption, even combined, are only an insignificant portion of the cost of child rearing. One of the experiences, I am told, which European Governments are coming upon is that the birth rate is continuing to decline. The belief is that this is largely because of the financial burden which potential parents or married couples perceive when they look at the cost of raising children and how it will affect their family budget, and when they consider the very nominal recognition of the tax system and social payments provided by their countries.
Family Allowances Act
Also 1 think we should look, in particular, at the position of the working poor. They are the people for whom family allowance is perhaps the most significant part of their budget, not in the sense of its being the largest part of their budget nor even in the sense of its being a larger part of the budget for them. These people will find that their incomes are not geared by another form of social support for the effects of inflation. These are the people who will in fact suffer most from the deindexing of family allowance payments.
The Government has chosen in its attack on the deficit to look really at just one side of the ledger. If there was ever a fault of which I thought the Tories would not be guilty it was failing to appreciate that there are indeed two sides to the national accounts; that there is an income side and an expenditure side. I think the fact that the Government has not brought in or reintroduced progressive tax rates, the fact that the Government has telegraphed reductions in taxes, exemptions, loopholes to the wealthy taxpayers of the country is as clear an indication as could be given of the fact that the Government is concentrating on expenditure reduction as the means of deficit reduction and is not looking at instituting in Canada the sort of fair tax system which would be both more productive in absolute terms and would provide a fairer sharing than exists today of the costs of providing benefits to our people.
Others have spoken and at some length on the principle of universality once espoused by the Prime Minister as a sacred trust. I believe that these reductions in family allowances that are predicated are indeed an erosion, a reduction of the principle of universality. That principle is important not only for philosophical but for pragmatic reasons. It is only when all can see some benefit from the system of social payments in this country that we will have the support of everybody in continuing to provide and co-operate in the mechanisms that provide those social assistance payments.
I am glad to hear my friends in the Liberal Party on side in this matter because when I heard their announcement of a so-called Operation Injustice a couple of days ago my first reaction was: Spare us! We have had the six and five program, that was Operation Injustice. Don't inflict that upon us again! But if the Liberal Party is prepared to go through the country and, ignoring its own history in this matter, help to bring the Opposition toward reduction in family allowances into this House, then I say, more power to them. I know that they will be pushing the same line and the same philosophy that the New Democratic Party is pushing and has always pushed.
I am glad to say that the psychology of charity has been almost eliminated from the social payments system in this country. I am glad to say that we can see ourselves as providers and as beneficiaries. I am concerned about the effect particularly on single-parent families, particularly on the poorest of the poor, that these reductions will have. I am glad to join my colleagues in the New Democratic Party and in the Opposition in voicing our opposition to those reductions.

September 17, 1985
Family Allowances Act

I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) for his question because, as he correctly observes, my constituency does contain the largest number of reserve communities of any constituency in Canada and I believe also the highest number of treaty Indian people of any constituency in Canada. The impact, quite frankly, in some communities where unemployment can run as high as 85 per cent in the winter time and can persist above the 50 per cent level all year, will be quite significant.
I have heard Members from the government side decry and deride this Party's opposition to these reductions on the ground that they are not really going to affect anybody. I can say with great certainty that there are people who are going to be affected, particularly when we look at the continuing cumulative effect of those reductions.
We know, considering the effect of inflation, that it will be 1988 before the real value of assistance payments to the poorest of the poor drops below what it is today. Simply because we are talking about a consequence that is three years down the line rather than an immediate consequence, 1 believe, does not give us the right to treat it any less seriously. The fact is that if it is in the Government's plans and prescriptions and programs that those people will function on a reduced income three years from today then we should discuss it with exactly the same weight as if it were to happen tomorrow.
Particularly for those women who are the heads of singleparent families with large numbers of children, they are certainly going to notice the difference in their family allowance cheque, particularly if the payments through the Canada Assistance Plan are not increased to make up for the reductions that they will experience. It will have a significant effect and I would call upon the Government to look at the effect upon the actual real life budgets of the poorest of the poor before this measure goes forward.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to say that your presence of mind is extraordinary.
Mr. Speaker, some mornings when everything goes wrong, we say to ourselves that we should have stayed in bed.
I think that Canadians, when they look back to what happened on September 4 last year, are saying that is exactly what they should have done on that particular morning.
However, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people are not to blame for the results we see today. Canadians have been misled by some very alluring election promises. It is like La Fontaine's fable about the Crow and the Fox, where the fox, after buttering up the crow, grabbed the cheese, exclaiming: "My dear fellow, you might as well learn that flatterers live off those who listen to them." The cheese, was a small price to pay for experience. The crow, embarrassed and ashamed, swore "never again".
Mr. Speaker, like La Fontaine's sly fox, the Conservative Party played on people's emotions and gained their confidence.
Family Allowances Act
Subsequently, it changed its position and is now refusing to give voters what it promised them.
Mr. Speaker, I do not like taking part in this kind of debate and I think it is very unfortunate that we are having one. We had a debate last spring on de-indexation of Old Age Security pensions and we thought at the time that the Government had finally gotten the message.

subsubtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The Conservatives are slow learners!

subsubtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Unfortunately, they did not get the
message.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps we should remind the Progressive Conservative Party, which has now formed the Government, what it promised us last year. I am not referring to election promises, because we know they have all been forgotten and that the Government has no intention of meeting those commitments.
I am speaking about a statement made on December 14, 1984, when the Right Hon. Prime Minister said to the press: "The federal Government has no intention of reducing family allowances for middle-income Canadians."
At the same time, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) dutifully stated that his role as Minsiter was to give signals and take initiatives to reinforce the role of the family and make it more meaningful in today's society.
Mr. Speaker, I would be the first to rejoice and to congratulate the Minister if he were to propose measures which favour the family. But we have to ask ourselves some questions.
By de-indexing family allowances, is the Minister strengthening the role of the family and the purchasing power of low and middle-income Canadians?
By de-indexing the child tax credit from 1990, is the Government guaranteeing the economic future of low and middle-income families and giving them opportunities to provide a decent education for their children?
By reducing the tax exemption for children from 1987, by forcing families to pay more taxes, and finally, by increasing the federal sales tax and oil taxes, is the Government reinforcing the economic power of families and making them more meaningful in our society? Mr. Speaker, there is only one answer to these questions: No, of course not!
The decision of the Government to take all these initiatives will only make low- and middle-income families poorer. This is obvious. By making cutbacks in all the programs aimed at families, the Government is reducing the income of these families and making life more difficult and much more expensive for them.
Mr. Speaker, I am not talking about abstract matters, but about harsh realities our families will have to face throughout the country and especially in New Brunswick.

September 17, 1985
Family Allowances Act
Even though the Budget suggests that, with those changes, assistance to lower-income families will be increased, it is a fact that a good number of lower-income families and all middle-income families with children will get less than they are now receiving under the current system. For instance, in the area of family allowances, a family now gets $375 a year per child; in 1986, it will get less because of the family allowances being de-indexed, and so forth in 1987, 1988 and 1989.
What must be understood in the Government proposals is that there is a long-term loss for families, despite the increase in the income tax child credit proposed for 1986, 1987 and 1988. However, concerning the income tax child credit, as early as 1990, that also will be de-indexed. Moreover, the other Budget proposals will in effect wipe out any benefit derived from the tax credit increase. Actually, in the next four years family benefits will rise slightly because of the increase in the income tax child credit. But starting in 1990, benefits will decrease and they will go on decreasing over the following years. This is because in 1990 the income tax child credit also will be de-indexed, just as family allowances are now. That is to say that the increase in those benefits will correspond to the increase in the inflation rate over and above 3 per cent.
If all things were to remain as they are now, the benefit increase would be 4 per cent rather than 1 per cent. Therefore, even if there is an increase, it will be slight and will not match the current inflation rate or cost of living increase.
This is not all. The Government has other proposals that are extremely unfavourable to families. Indeed, from 1986 on fewer families will be receiving the maximum income tax child credit.
The income ceiling which makes it possible for a family to receive the maximum Child Tax Credit is presently $26,330. But the Government proposes to lower this ceiling to $23,500. Therefore, all families whose income is between $23,000 and $26,000 will no longer be eligible to the Child Tax Credit.
Moreover, because the average salary will increase from year to year, more and more families will earn over $23,500 and get only reduced benefits. What is more, the personal income tax will increase in 1986.
Because of the generous proposals of the Tory Government ... I have still 10 minutes left, Mr. Speaker? Thank you. I thought a while ago that you were going to cut me short.
Because of the generous proposals of the Tory Government, the low- and middle-income family will loose its federal exemption beginning in 1986. Also, basic personal exemptions will be reduced, because they will be indexed from now only by the inflation rate exceeding 3 per cent instead of being fully indexed to the cost of living. The taxable income of the low-income family is therefore higher. So the Child Tax Credit will decrease, while the Income Tax and the Sales Tax will both increase.
In short, the future is far from being encouraging for low-and middle-income families.
Because of the budgetary measures, the poor families will get poorer and the rich families will definitely get richer.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister introduced this Bill, he asked us to understand it and to consider it in the light of the deficit, the national debt, and the Government's need to limit its expenditures. But if we take into account the great many families it is likely to affect, we should consider it in the light of the $2 billion granted to the oil multinationals, in the light of the exemption of capital gain taxes which benefit high income families, and in the light of the increased tax deduction resulting from greater RRSP investments. Low-income families do not benefit from these programs. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the poor will have to pay for what the rich no longer pay. It does not make sense and, above all, it is unfair! Is that the way the Government means to help those who need it most?
Mr. Speaker, the Government is taking steps which are both stringent and unfair. The Progressive Conservative Government wants to increase the burden of disadvantaged families. Yet, according to the 1981 census, 13 per cent of Canadian families live below the poverty line. In my own province of New Brunswick, the 16.2 per cent of the families living below the poverty line will be severely affected by the family allowance cuts. For all these families, Government money represents a major part of their income and helps them survive and make ends meet. As you know, Mr. Speaker, poverty unfortunately still exists in Canada. Perhaps you do not, but your neighbours know what it is to be poor and to live on a very small income. It is a situation nobody would wish to live or to impose on anybody else.
Nobody is proud to be poor or to admit being poor. Nobody lives on a small income out of choice or willingly. Life is not easy for everybody. All Canadians are not born in an affluent region or to a family who is well-off financially. Many Canadians live in isolated regions where the education system is limited to the primary and secondary levels and where employment is only seasonal. Mr. Speaker, seasonal employment means that a person will work up to 10 or 12 weeks during the summer months to become eligible to Unemployment Insurance benefits during the winter months. Which means that these families live on an extremely low income. If you work for 10 or 12 weeks on a salary of $400 and you live on Unemployment Insurance benefits the rest of the year, you do not earn all together more than $14,000.
But if you are not so lucky and earn only $250 a week over the first twelve weeks you will simply end up with a little over $12,000 a year. That is what it is like to be poor, to have limited means. One can pinpoint a poor family when attending parent-teacher meetings, or again at the first meeting before
September 17, 1985

school opens when parents are told: You will have to buy running shoes for your children, gym suits, dictionaries, various items the young need to attend school. And you can read their expression, those people are all sad because they have to make a choice as to what they can or cannot afford to buy for their children. It is unfortunate because not only will those children not have what others enjoy at school but they will not be able to participate in various activities such as minor hockey or figure skating. They are indeed pushed aside and that is what really hurts, to realize that one is not as well off as the others.
Mr. Speaker, all Hon. Members have to listen to their constituents to appreciate the fact that many of them have needs and that something has to be done about it.
Far from improving the living conditions of our constituents, the constituents of all the Members here, this Bill will make matters worse. It simply does not make sense, Mr. Speaker.
That is why I cannot let the Government have free reins. As we did last spring, we have to stop it or else the future of this country will be hopelessly jeopardized.
Mr. Speaker, I am giving this Government a very serious warning on behalf of the people of New Brunswick. I urge you to reconsider your position and not to reduce family allowances.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I most sincerely hope the Government will change its mind and do so before the people are forced to protest and demonstrate vigourously as they have shown they can during the debate on old age security pensions deindexation. The people of New Brunswick, both men and women, then joined forces with all other Canadians to tell the Government that it was being unfair. If need be, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to help them launch the same kind of demonstration to prove to this Conservative Government that this Bill is unfair.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, be now read a second time and referred to a legislative committee, and on the amendment of Mr. Frith (p. 6625).

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise today on the first anniversary of the swearing in of the new Government to join in the debate on second reading of Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family
Allowances Act, 1973, and the subsequent amendment. The Bill would provide for inflation protection for family allowance payments when the Consumer Price Index exceeds 3 per cent. It is unfortunate that the Opposition has chosen the strategy that it has. Rather than join a reasonable and necessary debate on this important subject, they have chosen to introduce an amendment to delay second reading for six months. This tells the people of Canada that the Liberals have put the issue on the backburner, that they refuse to participate in the debate, and that they are interested in nothing but political gain in a campaign of fear and misinformation. Of course, as always, they are eagerly joined in such a strategy by the NDP.
I now know that the Opposition Parties do not understand the simple fact that has been stated quite clearly by my fellow Manitoban, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) which cannot be ignored in any debate on any social program. That simple fact is that social programs and benefits cannot be separated from economic realities. There is at last a Government in Ottawa that understands this. The healthier the national economy, the stronger the social benefit system.
As we continue to undo the economic damage inflicted on Canada by the former Liberal Government, we must ensure that a greater proportion of benefits go to those in our society who are in the greatest need. In just one year we have started Canada's economy on the road to recovery. There are now 284,000 more Canadians working than there were a year ago. Unemployment is still at a level that is unacceptable, but it is a step in the right direction. Inflation is steady and low for the first time in many years. Over the past three years the federal debt grew at a rate of almost 25 per cent, which is almost three times the rate of growth of the GNP. With the current fiscal plan, debt growth should slow to 17.7 per cent this year and 14.6 per cent in 1986-87. Housing starts have increased to an annual rate of 155,000 units, up 24 per cent from the previous two quarters. And we have only just begun.
I suggest that there is not a Member in this House who does not know that we must provide more for the less fortunate Canadians. We are now attempting to do that in concert with a healthy economic recovery, and not with our heads in the sand alongside the Opposition Parties. Bill C-70 is a good start toward improving the social safety net in Canada. At the same time we must consider the further measures planned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to address the plight of low-income Canadians. Bill C-70 cannot be considered in isolation.
I refer the House briefly to page 43 of the Budget papers. I wish to refer to a few of the planned changes because they are so important to the debate on Bill C-70 and the amendment thereto. Beginning in the taxation year 1986 the child tax credit, payable in the spring of 1987, will be increased by $70 per child, from $384 to $454. In the taxation year 1987 the
September 17, 1985

child tax credit, which will be payable in the spring of 1988, will be increased by a further $35 to a total of $489. At the same time the child tax exemption will be reduced to $560 per child under age 18 at the end of the year. This makes the system much more progressive. For the taxation year 1988 the child tax credit will be increased a further $35 to a total of $524 per child under 18. At the same time the child tax exemption will be reduced to $470 per child under age 18 at the end of the year.
As you can clearly see, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-70 is just the first step in a series of changes that the Government is planning in response to the need for more benefits going to those most in need in Canadian society. The Government is looking to the future. We want to ensure the long-term health of our family benefit system, unlike the Liberals and NDP whose sole interest is short-term political gain at the expense of the very system they profess to be protecting. A delay of six months for second reading as proposed by the Opposition delays the beginning of changes to the system that are intended to improve the fairness of our family benefits system, and to ensure that maximum benefits go to families with children and with incomes of less than $25,000 per year. I keep hearing criticism from the Opposition on our proposal to introduce a capital gains exemption for individuals. They say that this is a proposal for the rich, but that is absolutely untrue. Among the number of Canadians who will benefit from this proposal are the farmers, the small businessmen, and the small town professionals who have worked hard and paid taxes to support our social benefits system.
"Private initiative" and "hard work" are not dirty words. People who have worked hard on family farms and in family businesses have been asking why they should work hard and take risks if the Government only penalizes them, as the former Liberal Government did. As a new Government we are going to reward hard work because we know that without these people we would soon have no social benefit system whatsoever. We have seen what the NDP Government in Manitoba thinks of small business and individual initiative. They slap on a special employment tax every time a business hires a new employee. That is some incentive; a tax on job creation.
I am also disturbed, Mr. Speaker, by a statement from the NDP spokesperson, the Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). In response to Bill C-70 she said that "it is easier to attack children than it is to attack old age pensioners". Can you imagine a statement such as this from an NDP Member of Parliament? It is truly incredible. New Democratic Party Members, who feel no remorse at all in supporting the death of thousands of unborn Canadian children, are telling us that we are attacking children with Bill C-70. Obviously the concern for children expressed by the NDP does not include the ultimate protection, that is, the right to be born. That subject deserves separate debate, but it does point out the serious contradiction in Opposition arguments.
My wife and three children are the most important part of my life and I have been fortunate enough to be able to provide
Family Allowances Act
for them. However, in my 13 years of work in the health care field, I have seen many families much less fortunate than mine. My family would not hesitate to give up part of the increase in the family allowance so that others in greater need would receive more.
In this debate we have also heard criticism from the Opposition Liberals on our recent changes to the devastating National Energy Program. Such statements prove their total lack of understanding with regard to western Canada. We were treated as a colony by the Liberals for so long that they have forgotten what they did to us. I would like to give a small piece of advice to the Liberals. If they ever hope to be credible in western Canada, they had better talk to westerners in order that they can understand that the Western Accord restores to the west what the Liberals took away with the National Energy Program. The Liberal spokesman, the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith), say that he is, "convinced that grandparents are concerned about what is happening to their grandchildren". I agree totally, but not because I want to enlist seniors in a fight against Bill C-70, but because seniors have a lot of experience and common sense and they worry about the future of their grandchildren. They can see through the cheap politics of the opposition and will join us in a long-term solution and a return to fairness in Canadian society and its social system.
In conclusion, I want to emphasize that Bill C-70 is only a first step in improving Canada's existing benefits system. When considered with plans to increase child tax credit payments, to make the child tax exemption more progressive within the tax system and to improve the system even more as the economy improves, I know that Canadians will support Bill C-70.
The effects of Bill C-70 will be twofold: first, the benefits to families will be distributed more fairly; second, there will be recognition of economic realities by all Canadian families. The Government supports the family and we are working to assure the future of family benefits. Everything cannot be done at once. As conditions improve and as the May 23 Budget continues to improve the Canadian economy, the family benefits package will be further improved. Therefore, 1 urge the House to defeat the amendment and pass second reading of Bill C-70 so it may be referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this crucial debate in the House of Commons. It is at least as crucial as the debate we had in the last session concerning pensions. We must examine very closely what the Government is proposing in the legislation before us. What is the purpose of the legislation and its effect? What exactly does it mean for Canadians?
First, it means there will be fewer dollars in mothers' pockets for the care of children. For a Government that speaks of having a strong economy in the future and for a Government that wants wise investment to take place in Canada, this is a short-sighted policy. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. White) said that the Government had a long view of events in Canada, that it was looking to the future and not just at today. If we are looking to the future and if we have a long-term view of social policy and of wealth creation in Canada, we should remind ourselves that one of the keys to that is human resources. Economists around the world are coming to that realization today. They have recognized
Family Allowances Act
that the creation of wealth is based on human resources and not simply on capital resources.
If this Government were looking at the long term, it would consider the impact of reducing family allowances as they affect investment in the development of our human resources. Our children, the children of every family in Canada, are the human resources of the future. They are the ones who will create the wealth. Adequate family allowances are an investment in those children and in the future of the Canadian economy but this Government is taking away dollars that would be invested through the measure before us.
This measure will put fewer dollars in the wallets of Canadian families for their children, and it is done by deindexing family allowances. Granted the deindexation is partial, but it is real, Mr. Speaker. If family allowances were to remain as they are today, families would receive an increase in their family allowance as the cost of living goes up. This is automatic, and the purchasing power of family allowances would be maintained. This does not mean families would be getting grand increases but by continuing indexation, the purchasing power is maintained rather than eroded. This measure will take money out of the pockets of ordinary Canadian families, contrary to the assertions of my colleague on my right-I might say on the far right, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
The purpose of the family allowance is to help mothers meet their children's needs.
We might ask ourselves whether there are any real needs of this sort to be met in the community. By way of illustration, let us consider nutrition. If a young child is to perform well in school, that child must have a balanced diet. Many children simply will not have that without adequate family allowances. A couple of weeks ago I was in Winnipeg and toured soup kitchens in my constituency. I talked to people preparing meals for those who have no other source of nutrition. Children have been seen on the streets of Winnipeg visiting the welfare agencies and the agencies which give out food because they do not have adequate food at home.
There are some very real needs of children that must be met. Family allowances are an attempt by the Canadian Government to meet those needs. It is not only in terms of having adequate food to eat that family allowances play a significant role, but they also have an impact with regard to human dignity and pride. Schools have just opened. Children like to have new clothes and new crayons to go to school. I was

September 17, 1985
Family Allowances Act
speaking to some workers in social service agencies in Winnipeg and they described how parents like to go out and buy new clothes for their children so a child can feel good on the first day of school because everyone is expected to have new clothes. These workers knew that because parents were buying new clothes they would be running out of welfare money used for food before the end of the month. There is a very real human need in terms of families who are on the lower end of the income scale. To these people family allowances are crucial. The family allowance is the foundation to our very existence. It is a symbol of hope. It is important for the Government to realize that when it cuts dollars from family allowances, the Government is taking money away from people who have some very real needs.
The family allowances perform another role having to do with the equality of women in our society. The family allowance is a cheque that goes in the name of the mother to assist her meet her children's needs. It recognizes the contribution a mother makes to the care of the children. It recognizes the value of her work.
More and more men these days are considering and taking up the option of full-time child care. It is to be applauded, but it is still a rare exception and the family allowance continues to be a way for the Canadian Government to recognize the value of the unpaid work of women in our society. It is a way that we as a society can acknowledge the importance of the time and energy which primarily women put into the care of children.
Not only does the action proposed by the Government take away dollars from families but it is a direct attack on the principle of universality in social programs. This is not the first time the Government has attacked universality. When it issued its economic statement early in its mandate, it raised questions about universality. Also it issued a policy paper and raised the same questions. However, more important, it attempted in its last Budget to deindex old age pensions partially. One would have thought that the Government would have learned from experience that an attack on the universality of social programs is a very risky undertaking because people realize the fundamental importance of universality.
It is important that social programs respect the dignity of all citizens and remove the negative stigma from receiving social assistance. When social programs are based upon income or need alone, people are required to prove that they are poor before they are eligible for social assistance. We know that society looks down upon those who are poor. Quite naturally people feel a sense of shame when they have to get down on their knees, so to speak, before the representative of a social agency to obtain an application for financial assistance. We are saying that the dignity of each person must be respected. Therefore, we are prepared to give social assistance to all citizens so that they know that they are receiving assistance as a matter of right, not because they are on the bottom rung of the social ladder. In order to respect human dignity in the
application of social programs, those programs have to be matched up with a fair tax system. If we have to raise revenues in order to continue such programs, we require a fair tax system so that people feel that it is only right and just to pay taxes because everyone else is carrying an equal share of the burden. In this regard, the Government is off the track. Rather than promote a fairer tax system in its recent Budget, it in fact made the system even more unfair. The best example of this would be the fact that as a result of the recent Budget, the average Canadian family will have to pay an increase of some $500 in taxes. At the same time the Government gave a write-off to upper-income Canadians of $500,000 under the capital gains proposal. Anyone with a great deal of capital will not have to pay taxes on the increase in the value of that capital. Those people with a great deal of wealth received a tax break while average Canadians were hit over the head with a significant tax increase.
The Government goes in the direction of attacking the universality of social programs and seeks to use selective social measures. It undermines the fairness of the tax system and its capacity to produce revenue. As a result, it finds itself in a corner with no alternative but to attack the universality of social programs.
Canadians value the universality of social programs. They demonstrated this when they beat back the attempts of the Government to attack the universality of pensions. We must match universality with a fair tax system and with an equitable economic policy. Rather than having as its objective the trickle down approach to economics, the Government should have employment for all as its major objective. The policy of the Government is to provide tax breaks for business and for upper-income Canadians in order to make it more "attractive" to invest. The assumption is that if there are fewer taxes on investment, there will be more investment, which automatically leads to more employment. Recently experience has demonstrated that that is false, that in fact the economy does not work that way. Over the last 20 years the burden of taxation on corporations relative to the burden of taxation on individuals has dropped significantly while its progressive nature has caused regression. As a result of this tax regime and the Government's economic policies, we have seen an increase in unemployment. The policy of the Government to make it more and more attractive economically for investors by lightening the taxation burden on them does not lead to the kind of economic growth which provides employment and therefore results in an equitable economic circumstance.
Along with universal social programs we need equity in economic policy. The primary objective of that economic policy must be to put all Canadians to work. We must co-ordinate all instruments at the disposal of the Government in order to reach that objective.
I want to examine briefly the performance of the Government since its election, particularly as it affects universality. Prior to and during the last election campaign, the Government described universality as a sacred trust. This so-called sacred trust has been torn to shreds. The one thing which
September 17, 1985

stands out in the minds of most Canadians today is that they can no longer trust the Government. Leading up to the election the Government made every effort to gain the confidence of Canadians, and the results of that election indicate that it obviously achieved this. However, since that time the Government has been rapidly losing the confidence of Canadians on the basis of its performance. On the one hand it promised to respect universality in social programs. On the other hand, as soon as it assumed office, it began a concerted attack on the universality of social programs. If there is one characteristic of this Government which stands out in the minds of ordinary Canadians, it is the fact that its performance is at variance with its promises. Therefore Canadians trust the Government less and less. While that has not yet been translated into large numbers in Gallup polls, that will come about. When Canadians lose confidence in their Government, there is no way that it can continue to hope for high levels of support in Gallup polls or in whatever other instrument exists for measuring the confidence of people in their Government.
In my remaining minute I should like to point out that the measure before us today should be withdrawn. It should be withdrawn because it takes out of the pockets of ordinary families across this country dollars which are necessary in order for children to have their basic human needs met. It should be withdrawn because it is a direct attack on the principle of universality. It should be withdrawn in order to sustain public confidence in the Government. The Government has lost and continues to lose the trust of Canadians by continuing this kind of action. We on this side of the House call upon this Government to withdraw the measure before this House, to respect its promises and to actually look for ways of improving social policy as it affects children rather than undermining them.
