PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT ACT, 1985 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-240, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to present this Bill in the House. I have conducted three surveys of my constituency and have found that between 85 per cent and 87 per cent of my constituents are in favour of the restoration of capital punishment. 1 remind you, Mr. Speaker, that in my riding there are approximately 5,000 police officers from Metropolitan Toronto and Durham, and their wives. 1 have been to the funerals of police officers from my riding. I have had hit home to me emotionally the trauma those families are under.
I would like to refer to one case of a young man in his twenties who pleaded with me before the 1979 election to take a stand on this issue. He told me all the reasons he was nervous about being a police officer. I went to his funeral. He died for the same reasons he told me he feared.
I call upon the House to reinstate capital punishment as an alternative to be available in cases of high treason and first degree murder. There is a certain provision in this Bill which states:
No person shall be convicted of first-degree murder upon the evidence of only one witness, unless the evidence of that witness is corroborated in a particular material by evidence that implicates the accused.
To be perfectly clear, I wish to stress the fact that this Bill would allow the sentence of the death penalty as an alternative only in cases where proof is 100 per cent verifiable. What we are trying to avoid here is evidence which may not be factual, which may be construed as being a fact but as not being accurate.
I would like to explain why the Criminal Code of Canada should be amended to reinstate capital punishment. A free but orderly society is dependent upon the entrenchment of well-known and established standards for acceptable behaviour. Capital punishment is an affirmation by the community that it views murder with abhorrence. It is this statement of revulsion, echoed in subtle ways from many directions during an entire lifetime, which helps dissuade the potential murderer from his act.
Restoration of the death penality will be a clear indicator that society is prepared to defend itself against mass murderers, serial murderers and murderers who carry out particularly vicious and deliberately cold-blooded or sadistic killings. Capital punishment underlines, as nothing else can, that murder is a serious business. Abolitionists ask if the return of the death penalty will make Canada a better place. I suggest that if we
continue along as we are going, taking good care of our murderers, we will subsequently extend an invitation to murderers from certain states below the border to make Canada their place of hiding.
I have also been very involved, Mr. Speaker, with victims of violence. In this connection, I feel we look after our murderers far better than we look after the victims and the families of victims. This invitation we are putting forward will surely be accepted, as in the case of Mr. Ng, as a recent editorial in The Globe and Mail pointed out. If we do not do something, we will attract those kinds of people to Canada and will have no jurisdiction to remove them. Does Canada wish to become a haven for the worst of U.S. society? Will that make Canada a better place? Most certainly not, Mr. Speaker.
Public opinion polls, and I have mentioned my own, have shown that since the 1970s an overwhelming majority of Canadians, at least 70 per cent, are in favour of reinstating capital punishment. Following the will of the people is what democracy is all about. Rehabilitation has become the ideal toward which we strive to the point at which retribution is in fact ignored. While I appreciate that rehabilitation is appropriate in many cases, Mr. Speaker, I believe that there are some crimes for which retribution must not be ignored. There are some acts, some crimes so terrible, so outrageous to public sensitivity that only the ultimate penalty will satisfy the need for rectification of the assault upon society.
I would like to address two of the major arguments used by abolitionists against capital punishment. They say that mistakes can be made. That is the one thing in framing this Bill that we were particularly careful about. Mistakes should not be made. The abolitionists state that people have wrongfully received the death penalty in Canada. This is not fact. They referred to Donald Marshall. He was charged on second degree murder so he was never subject to capital punishment.
The abolitionists also state that capital punishment is not a deterrent. Social scientists are actually divided on this issue. We could have a debate in this House for days, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think we could ever prove it one way or the other. The fact is that we will never know for certain how much of a deterrent capital punishment is or is not simply because we have no way in which to gather statistics on murders that never happened. The fact that the threat of capital punishment has not prevented some murders does not mean that it has not stopped others from happening.
I believe that it is our responsibility to take every precaution available to protect the lives of those who would become the innocent victims. Again, I speak on behalf of the victims who have been abused and who have not been taken care of. Hopefully, I will be presenting a Bill in this House on behalf of innocent victims.
In the case of premeditated murder, surely it can be assumed that the possible consequences of the Act are considered. It is also probable that the threat of the death penalty would discourage professional criminals for whom a stint in jail is an occupational hazard. Further, and in that connection, we have reviewed the situation of mandatory supervision. In
September 17, 1985

my own riding there have been murders committed by people out on mandatory supervision where the police force was not advised that those people had been realeased from jail. It is reasonable to assume that in seeking to avoid arrest, a criminal would be less likely to shoot a police officer if the result would be capital punishment. Common sense indicates that capital punishment must have some deterrent effect for the majority of human beings.
I would also like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the morality in our society is in a sad state. Young people are committing crimes which they did not commit 30 years ago. I believe we have to deal with the most severe criminals first and that there should be a ripple effect down to the minor criminal who starts off on the streets. I have talked to policemen whose lives are frustrated by minor criminal offences. They do not want to put these people in jail but there are no laws to help those people to be rehabilitated. We have a serious problem in Canada and it is getting worse. All one has to do is look at the insurance statistics to find out how bad it is. The morality in our society is in a sad state and I feel that by so dealing with the most severe criminals, perhaps it might have an effect on the behaviour of some Canadians.
As 1 mentioned earlier, if a potential murderer has been conditioned mentally by the existence of the most extreme form of punishment to be aware of the very serious consequences of his crime, he may avoid the criminal act. He may just realize that it is not worth it. By reserving this drastic punishment for the most serious crime, the law would foster a special abhorrence of murder in the minds of the public and this in itself would be expected to have some deterrent effect.
Allow me to reiterate, Mr. Speaker. Capital punishment does deter by fear of execution but that is not the only way. It also signals the revulsion of the community toward the crime and trains society to naturally abhore the crime.
We also hear other arguments, Mr. Speaker, that society has failed murderers in some way. Perhaps so. However, what are the chances of rehabilitating someone who fires a shotgun at point blank range into the face of an innocent victim? The officer I mentioned, the one who's funeral I went to, that is precisely what happened to him. I believe society has failed to entrench the utmost abhorrence for the most drastic offences as a fundamental principle of its foundation. Put another way, I ask if we have not failed the innocent victims? The young people, police officers and prison wardens, have we looked after them properly?
We also hear, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of Canadians are uninformed on the issue and incapable of making a reasoned judgment. That is why the statistics are so out of line, it is claimed. Some have used this argument to avoid the wishes of those it concerns. As I said before, I represent a large population of police officers in my riding. The reason is that many Metropolitan Toronto policemen live in my riding because they do not want to work where they live.
Capital Punishment
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, statistics show that between 1961 and 1981, the Canadian homicide rate rose by 116 per cent. This figure is usually given from the date of abolition in 1976. I am giving it to the House from the date when capital punishment was last imposed in Canada.
I would like to point out that some pretty crude methods of capital punishment have been used in the past. Better methods have been developed and that is why I suggested the use of a drug which has been proven by use in the United States and is administered by needle. It is humane and certainly not a crude method as we have faced in the past.
To go back to the statistics, I fully admit that the correlation does not imply causation and, therefore, we cannot say with certainty that the abolition of the death penalty has led to the increase in the homicide rate. The principle remains that we as a society must reaffirm our belief that life is sacred and the taking of a life with not be done cheaply, without retribution. I stand before you in this House today on behalf of my constituents and many other Canadians who have written to me from across Canada, including many police officers and prison wardens, and ask that this Bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to be given due consideration as it reflects the will of the people. 1 believe our Party is committed to bringing forward a Bill of this kind. I only ask that some of the thought which has gone into this Bill be brought to the attention of the committee. 1 realize we will have our opportunity but I have a responsibility to a large constituency of approximately 150,000 people, as well as a responsibility to the police officers who protect these people. I am certain that the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) is working to develop the Bill and bring it forward. I started my Bill as soon as the House reconvened in September, 1984, and I have now had my opportunity to bring it forward. I repeat that I would really appreciate the opportunity of having this Bill referred to the standing committee where it can be thoroughly studied and reviewed.

Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable regret and chagrin that I participate in this particular debate. At the outset I would like to state my position and state it clearly for the record. My constituents are well aware of the fact that I do not support capital punishment and that, as a parliamentarian, I intend to use every means conceivable to stop any effort by any Member of this House or the Government to restore capital punishment. I am opposed to capital punishment for a number of reasons. First and foremost, I am opposed because of my moral conviction and my attitude toward human life. In my view human life is sacred and regardless of how miserable a human life may be, regardless of what criminal act an individual commits, it is my firm belief that no person other than the Creator, no person and no state, should take the life of an individual.
Hon. Members are aware of my position with respect to abortion. I have stated in this House my unequivocal opposition to abortion because of the fact that human life is sacred and because I do not believe that any state should take the life of an individual. There are those Members opposite and others

September 17, 1985
Capital Punishment
who might suggest that I should be representing my constituents. I freely admit that a large majority of my constituents are in favour of capital punishment. There is no question about that and I am sure it is the same for all Members of this House. However, I do not feel bound by the views of my constituents on this particular issue and if I offend some because of the position I take, I apologize to them. However, I would like to quote Edmund Burke, speaking to the electors of Bristol on November 3, 1774. He said: "Your representative owes you not his industry only but his judgment and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it to your opinion." I am exercising my judgment, Mr. Speaker, and my commitment and belief in the position 1 take on this issue.
In 1976, when Parliament abolished capital punishment, we as a nation became civilized; we as a nation became moral; we as a nation said to our people and to the people of the world that it is wrong, barbaric and grotesque to take the life of another human being. That debate took place nine years ago and, yes, there have been those who have clamoured for the return of the death penalty over the past nine years. To its credit, Parliament has resisted and I am sure Hon. Members in this House who were present in 1976 will recall that debate and how close the vote was. It carried by a six or seven or eight vote margin. It was a difficult time for Members of Parliament. It was a difficult debate which went on for 95 or 96 hours. To its credit, this Parliament abolished capital punishment and it was thought at the time that it was abolished once and for all. However, much to the chagrin of not only Canadians, but the world, Canada is now reconsidering the issue. The Government has committed itself to a free vote. During the last election campaign it promised that it would have a debate in the House of Commons. To his credit, and that of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and others, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is opposed to it. 1 ask why in God's name we should be debating this issue again here today. What is the justification?
In an explanatory note in this Bill it is indicated that:
The purpose of this Bill is to restore the death penalty for first degree murder and high treason, while substituting a more humane mode of execution for hanging.
What is humane about taking another life? There is no humane mode of killing another human being. It is easy, I suppose, for some Members to argue for the death penalty. I suggest that some are reading the polls and playing politics.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member opposite says, not I. Indeed, not I. I am standing here speaking before this House and to my constituents, notwithstanding that my constituents, and the overwhelming majority of Canadians, are in favour of capital punishment. If political defeat is the result of the position I take on capital punishment, so be it, because I, as an individual, am not prepared to compromise some very basic principles. I cannot compromise my soul because of any public
opinion poll. There are those who are looking at the polls and those polls are dictating how they should vote on this particular matter. I ask those Members who look at the polls to sit back and search their souls and ask themselves whether they truly believe that the state should take another life. Hon. Members opposite nod and say yes. That is their right and prerogative. They can do it. They can call for capital punishment, but I simply ask those who are not as committed as the Hon. Member who has proposed this Bill and have not come to a definite conclusion with respect to this particular issue, to look at the facts and search their souls because this is an important issue. It is not important simply because Canadians say it is important, but because it deals with human life. It will undoubtedly be the most important decision that we parliamentarians make during this Parliament.
Why capital punishment? The Hon. Member has given some reasons. He has indicated that a great number of Canadians support capital punishment, but it is my respectful submission that a great many Canadians, including those in my constituency of York South-Weston, perhaps do not understand the ramifications and fully comprehend the fact that capital punishment is not a deterrent. Study after study has concluded that capital punishment is not a deterrent.
Before I get into the statistics to substantiate my submission that it is not a deterrent, I would like to quote a passage from an essay called "A Hanging" written by George Orwell in 1931 and set in Burma. I think it comes closer than anything else I have ever read in conveying what it means to execute, to kill, to murder a human being. Orwell writes:
It was about forty yards to the gallows. I watched the bare brown back of the prisoner marching in front of me. He walked clumsily with his bound arms, but quite steadily, with that bobbing gait of the Indian who never straightens his knees. At each step his muscles slid neatly into place, the lock of hair on his scalp danced up and down, his feet printed themselves on the wet gravel. And once, in spite of the men who gripped him by each shoulder, he stepped slightly aside to avoid a puddle on the path. It is curious, but till that moment I had never realized what it means to destroy a healthy, conscious man. When I saw the prisoner step aside to avoid the puddle, I saw the mystery, the unspeakable wrongness, of cutting a life short when it is in full tide. This man was not dying, he was alive just as we were alive. All the organs of his body were working- bowels digesting food, skin renewing itself, nails growing, tissues forming-all toiling away in solemn foolery. His nails would still be growing when he stood on the drop, when he was falling through the air with a tenth of a second to live. His eyes saw the yellow gravel and the grey walls, and his brain still remembered, foresaw, reasoned-reasoned even about puddles. He and we were a party of men walking together, seeing, hearing, feeling, understanding the same world; and in two minutes, with a sudden snap, one of us would be gone-one mind less, one world less.
We have to ask ourselves what conceivable purpose capital punishment will serve. It is not a deterrent as I will try to show in my submission. It is an attempt by some to extract their pound of flesh, to extract their vengeance. It is simply state-sanctioned vengeance, retribution. Our criminal justice system simply cannot be based on vengeance and retribution; an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. We are beyond that. That is barbaric, that is history, that is the mark of an uncivilized nation and of uncivilized people. We have gone beyond that. There must be some real justification for our criminal justice system. If Members opposite and others could prove to me and others that capital punishment is a deterrent, then I would.
September 17, 1985

suggest they might be standing on firmer ground. However, they cannot do that. Even Chief Ed Lunney of the Edmonton police force concedes the studies that say capital punishment is not a deterrent.
Canadian and American statistics show that capital punishment is not a deterrent. In 1975, the year before Parliament repealed the death sentence, there were 701 homicides, including murder, manslaughter and infanticide. In 1983, seven years after abolition, there were 682 homicides. The more important statistic is the rate of homicides per 100,000 population. In 1975, again, the year before capital punishment was abolished, Canada's homicide rate was 3.09 per 100,000. By 1983, it had fallen to 2.74. Is that evidence of capital punishment being a deterrent?
Those who argue that capital punishment is necessary to protect policemen are also without supporting evidence. In the five years before abolition, 19 policemen in Canada were murdered, compared to 18 in the five years after abolition. These are the facts.
If we look south of the border, again there are statistics that clearly indicate that capital punishment is not a deterrent. At present there are 38 states in the United States that have capital punishment on the books. Among western countries, only Ireland, Liechtenstein and 38 states of the United States retain capital punishment for the crime of murder. Britain abolished capital punishment in 1965. Since then, the British Parliament has reconsidered the question and, to the credit of British parliamentarians, they again said no to capital punishment. In 1981 the French Government abolished capital punishment. Now we in Canada, in this haven of safety-if I may say so-are considering bringing back capital punishment. It is a black mark on our country and it will be a dark day if this country ever decides to reinstate capital punishment.
Let me return to the statistics. As I said, in the United States, 38 states have the death penalty. The homicide rate in the United States is 8.3 compared to our figure of 2.7 homicides per 100,000 citizens. Where would Hon. Members rather live-in the United States or Canada? We have a safer country, even though we do not have the death penalty. Our rate is 2.74 compared to 8.3.
The Americans have not been reluctant to carry out executions since the Supreme Court of the United States decided that capital punishment was not cruel and unusual punishment. Three thousand nine hundred people have been executed in the United States since 1930. Some of those were Canadians.
One of the most interesting facts about capital punishment in the United States is that those states that have sentenced the most people to death and have actually carried out the most executions tend to be the states that have the worst murder records. Most of the worst rates are concentrated in the southern states where nearly two-thirds of all death row prisoners are held. Figures from the Federal Bureau of Investigation for 1983 show Louisiana and Texas tied for the worst

Texas ranks third in the nation in the number of people executed since the FBI began collecting national statistics in 1930, with 298 executions. There were 367 executions in Georgia and 329 in New York.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we are considering a Bill that proposes to reintroduce capital punishment for the offence of treason and first degree murder. I am certainly very sympathetic to the views of the Hon. Member who introduced the Bill and who expressed his very deep concern about the loss of life of one police officer in particular. I think we are all very sympathetic to the situation of police officers and prison officers who are the ones who risk their lives on our behalf and are amongst those arguing for a reintroduction of the death penalty.
However sympathetic I am with the intention of the Hon. Member and indeed of the police associations and correctional associations which advocate the return of capital punishment, I cannot be at all sympathetic with their concrete proposal that the reintroduction of the death penalty will give any additional safety to police officers, prison officers or any citizens as they go about their business.
It simply is not a fact that the death penalty deters. There has been abundant evidence about this in many studies. The United Nations has produced evidence of many countries over many years that have abolished capital punishment, reintroduced it and then changed the circumstances. It does not seem to be the case that capital punishment is any general deterrent against the offence of murder or any particular deterrent for those who must work with convicted persons or deal with them as police officers.
The death penalty was abolished in Canada and the murder rate actually declined after its abolition. One might even argue that citizens would be at greater risk with the reintroduction of the death penalty since its abolition has had some success. In any event, we are not a highly violent society. I believe that comparisons to the United States and the influence from the United States where the death penalty has been reintroduced give a very false picture.
Our murder rate is less than half that in the United States; fortunately, we are not nearly as violent a society here. Therefore, we should not be influenced by the much greater sense of panic and desperation felt by people in the United States in coping with the crime problems there.
If deterrent is not a logical argument in favour of capital punishment-which it really is not-what other reasons have been offered for the reintroduction of capital punishment? A number have been given, including the principle, "Eye for an
6722

September 17, 1985
Capital Punishment
eye, tooth for a tooth and life for a life". It is the idea that retribution is an honourable, proper and indeed just requirement. It is the argument that capital punishment is a religious principle and that there are reasons from our own religion to justify the reintroduction of capital punishment. Indeed, surveys tell us that people who hold a religious faith are more likely to be in favour of capital punishment than those who do not hold a religious faith. To one who does hold a religious faith, I find this a very shocking and disturbing fact. However, it is interesting to note that the churches themselves are becoming very active in the debate on capital punishment and coming out very strongly against the restoration of capital punishment as a matter of principle.
Let me cite some material prepared by the Interchurch Taskforce on Responsible Alternatives to the Death Penalty, produced by the Canadian Council of Churches which represents a very important cross-section of the churches in Canada. Let me quote from what they call "The Religious Viewpoint':
The continued abolition of capital punishment is officially supported by Catholic, Protestant and Jewish bodies, as well as by many organizations concerned with the justice system in Canada. Some Christians claim that the death penalty is needed to uphold the sanctity of human life: they rely on the Old Testament warrant, "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed,-But Christ's teaching stresses mercy and reconciliation. When they brought him the woman taken in adultery (then a capital crime), Christ did not deny the penalty under the law but only said, "He that is without sin, let him cast the first stone.4
That is a pretty clear teaching. The Viewpoint goes on:
Those who have experienced God's forgiving love must act on God's promise of power to redeem broken situations and people.-How can adding another broken body balance the scales of justice?
How, indeed? There is no way that capital punishment restores a life that has been taken and there is no abstract way in which this loss of life can be set aright by the taking of another life.
Let me quote again:
Violence as public policy only adds to the cycle of violence, vengeance, and destruction. We should never give up on a fellow human being. To love someone who has murdered is a demanding test of our faith. Since God "desireth not the death of a sinner, but rather that he may turn from his wickedness and live", we should follow the divine example.
That is a very radical teaching, and perhaps it is one too radical for the Parliament of Canada. It is one on which I think all Christian people should reflect very seriously when they want to use the notion of divine retribution as a justification for the human penalty of capital punishment.
Let me quote also from the statement by the Archbishops and Bishops of the Anglican Church of Canada, which is my own denomination. This is a very strong statement against capital punishment. It reads:
We urge our people and Members of Parliament that they consider seriously the implications of re-introducing the death penalty and not give in to a hasty response-These implications include such things as: the impossibility of reversing the hanging where there has been a miscarriage of justice-
We do know that there are miscarriages of justice. It continues:
-the ignoring of evidence concerning the ineffectiveness of the death penalty as a deterrent-
I think that has been aptly demonstrated. It continues:
-a belief that the murderer is beyond being changed by God's grace to be a creative member of society.
We are convinced that it is in the best interests of Canadian society as a whole that capital punishment not be re-introduced, but that as Christians we need to seek alternatives that recognize the infinite worth of the individual before God.
Mere incarceration without rehabilitation will not change the murderer. Reform of our correctional systems needs to become a priority of our Government.
I think that is putting it in a very whole context as to what the principles are and what our responsibilities ought to be. Let me make it very clear when I have been citing some Christian authorities on this I do not wish to suggest that the Old Testament examples should be taken, as they are very often used, as an unequivocal demand for human retribution as a consequence of breaking the law.
In the Old Testament times capital punishment was certainly permitted and required for a very large number of offences, but there was still a very important array of conditions that limited the use of capital punishment. The standard of proof required for conviction amounted to certainty. It was required that there be more than two adult male witnesses, a much more severe requirement for evidence than in any of our laws or what is in the Bill before us today.
Further, the Mosaic law had, as the penalty for perjury, execution itself, a very severe punishment for anyone who would give false evidence to convict a person, a much stronger provision against perjury to ensure that any evidence given in a murder case would be correct evidence. In difficult cases, the verdict was deferred to judicial experts who had to go to a different venue to reconsider the matter. In short, a very important number of conditions that would considerably have qualified the imposition of capital punishment in any case. Therefore, when people simply quote all the available opportunities for the use of capital punishment in the Old Testament, they must consider that the possibility of their being used would have been very, very severely constrained. How many instances would there really be of multiple witnesses, eye witnesses, adult males who gave evidence in the proper fashion and all of the proceedings were correctly gone through?
There are other examples one can site. Quoting from the Book of Deuteronomy:
To me belong vengeance and recompense.
And from Leviticus:
You shall not take vengeance.
There are all kinds of instances that we are told it is not necessary or proper for human persons to exact human vengeance. The first murderer appearing in the Old Testament, Cain, was not executed. His life was protected. So much for a very bloodthirsty rendition of the Old Testament as a good justification for the reinstatement of capital punishment.
September 17, 1985

Let us examine some of the provisos that have been proposed in the Bill before us today. It is the Hon. Member's intention that there be very selective use and careful measures taken. He referred to 100 per cent reliability. I would respectfully suggest that it is not possible to have 100 per cent reliability. His Bill said there would have to be more than one witness or if one witness, that there be corroborating material evidence. I do not quite know what he means by this witness. Is it going to be an actual eye witness to the murder? I wonder how many cases would be covered. We also know about eye witnesses. There have been instances of mistakes being made even with eye witnesses. It seems unlikely, but it has happened. We have instances of people being hanged or otherwise executed who have been subsequently found not to have committed the murder in question.
There is even the matter of having material corroborating evidence, and I think of a recent British case where there was a handful of hair in the victim's hand. Many years later it was found it could not have been hair from the convicted person because new scientific tests had been developed which made that identification possible. At the time of the trial, the material evidence was extremely convincing that the person convicted was the murderer. It sounds all very good in theory to talk about material corroborating evidence and eye witnesses, but we do know that mistakes will be made and there is no way of having an absolutely safe system.
I want to get a little more broadly into the issue of violence. I suggest that capital punishment is not going to help deter the offence of murder or treason. We do have too much violence in our society, even if our society is not as violent as that in the United States and in many other countries. Naturally we could all like to see a reduction in violence.
I wonder why we are focusing so much on murder and not spending our time more constructively in looking at other causes of violence and other measures which this Parliament could be taking. I refer to the issue of violent pornography on which we have had an enormous amount of stalling. Proposals have been made. I have been active in the struggle over a number of years. This Parliament is very slow to act. Here is an opportunity where we could change the context, change the reality in which people do commit murder. We have all kinds of practical things we could do about such things as husbands who beat their wives and children. There are far more things to be done by way of prevention, such as counselling services, group discussions, all kinds of practical measures to develop a spirit of co-operation and non-violent solutions to problems. It would be far more useful for us to be discussing these measures which possibly could have some practical impact and could actually reduce the level of violence in society.
Far more people are killed unnecessarily by other means. For example, roughly 5,000 people per year are killed in traffic accidents, and roughly half of these deaths is the responsibility of drunk drivers. That is far more than the murder rate. However, practical measures to reduce the number of drunk
Capital Punishment
drivers and practical measures to enforce the laws in a stricter fashion are shunted aside; they do not seem to be so important. Also a large number of people die in industrial accidents as a result of negligence. People debate whether it is criminal negligence or non-criminal negligence, but it certainly is very wrong. They are violent, preventable deaths. They occur in much larger numbers than murder by one person in a deliberate fashion of another. Also there are large numbers of deaths of people as a result of exposure to low levels of radiation. This is not dramatic; it happens over time. It is not someone shooting or knifing someone else, yet the number of deaths caused in this fashion is very much greater. Also I could refer to the number of fires and deaths which are caused inadvertently by people who are careless smokers. Again the number is very large and many of these instances are preventable.
I do not think we as a society are helpless or that we have to accept a large number of unfortunate but "nothing can be done about it" deaths. We could be acting constructively to reduce many other forms of violence in society.
In conclusion, I suggest that capital punishment is a false solution to a problem. We are spending our time debating capital punishment, a relatively modest problem within the context of the world and within the context of other preventable causes of death in society. We are taking time away from much more practical activity which could be socially much more beneficial.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT ACT, 1985 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
I would like to comment today on Bill C-240 sponsored by the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell).
Many of us have had an opportunity to speak to this topic during discussions in the House on the reinstatement of provisions relating to capital punishment. The problem is a very complex one. It raises questions about our personal convictions and philosophy, our concepts of justice and of what constitutes fair and equitable punishment for certain crimes.
However, although it may be difficult to avoid getting involved in philosophical considerations, nevertheless, it may be useful to aim for a more objective assessment of the issue.
Mr. Speaker, there are several subjects that can provide the neutral terrain favourable to the kind of discussion we wish to undertake. Some of these have already been suggested by a number of my colleagues in this House. Today, I would like to talk about international conventions.
At the international level, there has been for several years a growing concern for humanizing penal justice. The United Nations, for instance, has been making a sustained effort to obtain fair treatment for prisoners and inmates and to prevent abuse in the penitentiary system. As an example of these efforts I would like to quote certain provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: everyone has the right to be presumed innocent "until proved guilty according to law in a public trial at which he has had all the guarantees necessary

September 17, 1985
Capital Punishment
for his defence", or for instance, "no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment."
Mr. Speaker, there is also the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, whose aim is to ensure recognition, respect and protection of our fundamental rights and dignity, and especially of persons who are deprived of their freedom. Finally, I would like to mention other international agreements such as the Declaration on the Protection of All Persons Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, and the Draft Resolution prepared by the Committee on the Prevention of Crime and Treatment of Offenders, which concerns guarantees for the protection of the rights of a person subject to the death penalty, both aimed at protecting the rights and dignity of prisoners and persons who have been convicted.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that in Canada as in other countries, our national law takes precedence. Thus, draft legislation that would not be in line with internationally recognized aims would not as a result become illegal. However, by signing international conventions or agreements, Canada has expressed its willingness to apply these principles and to consider them when preparing and implementing its own legislation. For instance, when interpreting our Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, we could draw on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Furthermore, the purpose of the ratification by Canada of an international convention or covenant is to make their provisions binding on the federal and provincial governments vis-a-vis other signatory countries. Canada, for instance, ratified the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and any contravention by Canada of the provisions of this covenant would be perceived as a violation of its international obligations.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, Canada is bound by these international conventions and agreements, at least to a certain extent. We must take them into account in our legislation. And so, when we are discussing the reinstatement of capital punishment, we must take into consideration the various agreements to which we have given our support in the past. Unfortunately, the Bill before the House today does not entirely conform to these agreements and conventions.
The first point I want to make in analyzing Bill C-240 concerns procedural guarantees. In other words, the procedural rules that are to protect the rights of the accused.
Mr. Speaker, international agreements put a great deal of emphasis on the right of everyone to adequate representation before the courts. By adequate representation we mean the right to have the necessary time to prepare a good defence as well as the right to be represented by an attorney of one's own choice. A lot has also been said about the right to appeal to a higher court in cases where a sentence has been handed down. In the case of a death sentence, the latest international position which Canada is committed to consider as a result of the Sixth
United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders provides that the appeal is automatic and mandatory. In cases where the accused is punishable by death, international agreements contain provisions concerning the burden of proof. A draft resolution of the Committee on the Prevention of Crime and the Prevention of Criminality, which Canada has endorsed, recommends that the death sentence be carried out, and I quote:
"only when there is absolutely no doubt whatsoever that the person accused of a crime is guilty, on the basis of clear and convincing evidence which does not leave room for any other interpretation of the facts."
Finally, still with respect to procedural guarantees, the international agreements also emphasize clemency and commutation of sentence. Certain people acknowledge that any person sentenced to death has the right to ask for commutation or to petition for mercy on his or her own behalf.
Does Bill C-240 contain all the guarantees I have just mentioned? For starters, Mr. Speaker, this Bill does not have any provision concerning adequate representation for the accused before the courts. Although this principle is spelt out in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, not only does it need to be stressed but as well the participation of an attorney in the defence of any person accused of a crime punishable by death ought to be made mandatory. In such a case the seriousness of the punishment fully warrants the provision of clearly expressed guarantees just so there will be no doubt that the accused has the best defence available.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT. (B) APPOINTMENT OF CANADA ENVOY
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT. (B) APPOINTMENT OF CANADA ENVOY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity today to follow up on a question I asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) shortly after his Shamrock Summit meeting with President Reagan in March.
You will recall that at that time when the Prime Minister became so famous for his rendition of When Irish Eyes are Smiling that I suggested in the House that if we did not see more action on acid rain than we had coming out of the Shamrock Summit, at the same time next year we could all join the Prime Minister in a chorus of Raindrops Keep Falling
September 17, 1985

on my Head, referring of course to the continuing problem of acid rain. I might also suggest that another appropriate tune for what has been going on over so many years with respect to acid rain would be the song that was a hit a number of years ago called Killing Me Softly With His Song.
What is happening here and what is happening to our lakes in Canada has everything to do with the quiet way in which the life in many of our lakes and streams is being extinguished over the course of time by the continuing inaction on the part of Governments with respect to acid rain. I think the new Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) said it very well a couple of days ago, that politicians have essentially been asleep at the switch.
I think it is fair to say also that not all politicians have been asleep at the switch and there have been voices at the political as well as at the scientific level over the years which have called upon Governments to recognize that this was a problem, and to act, and that those voices have gone largely unheeded. Now it appears that indeed attention may be paid to them, and that is a good sign.
What has happened since I asked that question on March 19? A number of things have happened. Here in the House we have formed a special committee on acid rain on which I have the honour to serve as the New Democratic Party Member. That committee recently had the opportunity to meet in the Muskoka area with the two special envoys on acid rain, the former Premier of Ontario, Mr. William Davis, who is the special envoy of the Prime Minister and Mr. Drew Lewis, the special envoy of President Reagan with respect to acid rain. We had the opportunity to meet with those two gentleman in Muskoka for a couple of hours to discuss their work and the ways in which we might co-operate on the problem of acid rain and I must say, as one who was initially cynical and remains to a degree cynical about the envoy process I was nevertheless encouraged by what Mr. Lewis had to say about the direction he thought his report would be going and about the kind of advice he might be giving to the President with respect to acid rain. I was particularly encouraged that there did not seem to be any debate any longer, at least in Mr. Lewis's own mind, about there being a problem and about the need for action. If that could become an incontestable political fact in in the United States, that would be a victory for us and I hope that sort of thing will be forthcoming.
With respect to the Canadian envoy, Mr. Davis, my over-all impression was that he was far too relaxed about the subject and not as intense or as passionate about the need for action as I would like to have seen. That may be a question of style, it is too early to judge, and I hope that the former Premier will prove me wrong when he makes his report.
I am, however, concerned about reports which came out the day after the special committee met with Mr. Lewis and Mr. Davis, reports having to do with the budget which Mr. Davis received for his acid rain work. There was a report to the effect that the over-all cost of Mr. Davis' appointment would be in
Adjournment Debate
the neighbourhood of $500,000 and that, quite understandably, a great deal of that money would have to do with travel and accommodation. However, a great deal was also going toward his own personal staff, which is handling not just work pursuant to his responsibilities as Special Envoy for Acid Rain, but also his own personal business having to do with the variety of corporations on whose boards he serves. I am concerned about this.
I know that the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain is also concerned about it because they do not want to see the whole issue of acid rain dragged down to the level of those arguments which go on about the nature of political patronage in this country. They certainly do not want Mr. Davis to be seen as a patronage appointment. I want to register their concern and my concern to the Government, and through the Government to Mr. Davis, that when he brings down his report, in every way possible it should be of a quality which will justify the money spent, so that we will know when it comes down that some of the concerns I have expressed before, and which others have expessed, about Mr. Davis' appointment will be proven wrong. We would be glad to be wrong on this matter, Mr. Speker. I just hope that the Government is taking every step now to ensure, with respect to the report on Mr. Davis' budget, that the money being spent in the name of acid rain is, in fact, being spent on that very issue.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT. (B) APPOINTMENT OF CANADA ENVOY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), I think the Hon. Member ended with a somewhat regrettable tone. I will deal with that in a moment. For now, I would like to come to the substance of his representations.
It has been a long time, indeed, since he first asked the question and a great many events have taken place in the interim. I appreciate his mentioning the fact that our current Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has indicated the high priorities acid rain has with this Government. 1 think this has been done with honesty in terms of how actions have not been taken over a long period of time by governments and politicians in the past in spite of the fact that there are some who have had a keen sense of awareness of the problem.
The issue boils down to identifying for the record several points which I believe are important. First, in February of 1985 a commitment between the federal Government and the provincial Governments for the apportionment of deposition in each area of Canada was gained so that our desired level of 20 kilograms per hectare per year could be reached. We then followed that up with a number of specific actions, including the sub-committee reinstatement and actual funds which were put toward the cost of control in Canada and so on. We have been doing this work in Canada. In fact, we have been seen to be doing our homework.
We were left with the serious problem which has been in existence ever since 1979 when the first memorandum of intent was signed with the United States. We have had, in fact, an impasse which could not be overcome. That impasse had to be dealt with in some way. I think that we were fortunate to

September 17, 1985
Adjournment Debate
have been able to provide a break, if you like, in what seemed to be a firm boundary which had been drawn around the issue from Canada's point of view and from the point of view of the United States. Through the appointments of Mr. Lewis and Mr. Davis, I think we have a serious opportunity to see that impasse broken down. I know the Hon. Member was pleased, as were we, to see that Mr. Lewis was thinking seriously of making specific recommendations, not only in terms of abatement control now, but in terms of dealing with the whole issue on a long-term basis so that we can accomplish the entire chore which we set out to accomplish.
I have to take some exception to the allusions which have been made, not only in the newspaper article, but also here in the House of Commons, insofar as Mr. Davis is concerned. We in Canada had at the time that Mr. Davis was appointed a need for someone of his stature, his experience and, in fact, someone in whom the United States would have confidence, to carry the ball for us at that level. Mr. Davis happened to be available. I cannot account directly, Mr. Speaker, for the proportion of finances Mr. Davis has used and where they fall in terms of travel, office expenses and so on. I would have to challenge the Hon. Member to tell me if he has never had his secretary make a personal call for him. I believe the Canadian public should know-and in most ways do know-that not only is the job itself so serious and important that the actual amount spent by the envoys is very small indeed in comparison, but that both Mr. Lewis and Mr. Davis are working for $1 dollar a year. I do not know how many Members of Parliament would do that.
There are things which have to go on in the meantime. Life goes on for people who are dedicating themselves; to the extent of energy and effort which both Mr. Lewis and Mr. Davis have put into this effort. If there were calls made on behalf of Mr. Davis for the scheduling of other things, I really wonder whether the Hon. Member thinks that that is a serious affront to the sense of propriety we would all like to have. Unless the Hon. Member and other members of the press want to continue to try to raise the issue from this point of view, I do not believe it in any way jeopardizes the respect which the Americans will have for the efforts of Mr. Davis and the respect which we all should have for the contribution he is making on behalf of Canada in trying to come to firm grips with the acid rain problem.

Mr. Speaker, on June 27 I pressed the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) to take action to ensure that the Canadian shipbuilding industry might again experience prosperity. The immediate focus of my question was the threat of bankruptcy facing Halifax Industries Limited, a matter about which some action was eventually taken. However, I noted the plight of the shipbuilding industry generally.
This is an industry which is in distress and which is baffled by the failure of the Government to act on promises made during the last election campaign to create a more viable and prosperous Canadian shipbuilding industry. The Minister said that he did not plan to let months and months pass before doing something. Today it is 10 days short of three months since he gave that response and we are still awaiting his announcement of measures to create a prosperous shipbuilding industry.
The last days have produced mixed signals for the industry. Ontario shipyard operators and workers, who appreciate the recent decision of the Department of National Defence to allow them to share in refitting work on Canada's aging naval vessels, are distressed to think that the Department may change its mind on this issue. In my own riding, Port Arthur shipbuilding, which is primarily involved in repair work, is one of the yards very concerned about the possibility of the Department going back on that recent decision.
The Government's decision last week to order the construction of the Polar Class 8 icebreaker for year-round service in the Arctic, on the other hand, will create a significant amount of work, possibly in more than one yard. However, the decision was in response to Canadian sovereignty considerations rather than reflective of any developing industrial strategy, or at least there has been no evidence to suggest that it was not primarily those sovereignty considerations which guided the Government.
I would suggest that as the Government continues to consider this matter and, hopefully, comes to an early decision, the possibility that an industrial strategy might be initiated by Government construction is a subject which should be immediately before the Ministers involved. The Canadian patrol frigate program for our navy, the construction of icebreakers of various sorts, the construction of ferries for CN Marine in particular, provide examples of construction which the Government directly or through corporations can carry on. By doing that on a reasonable schedule the Government could ensure that yards are kept at work and that technical capacity in the form of computer assisted design and manufacturing is built into our yards. By keeping the yards at work we could ensure that we have the necessary shipbuilding capacity for the future.
I would suggest that an important part of that approach needs to be the ship construction for Maritime Command. As we realize more and more the state of our navy, it becomes obvious there are many vessels to replace. That can certainly be a part of such a program.
However, the shipbuilders are anxious that their business not be based solely on Government orders. I quite appreciate their desire for a large volume of commercial construction. 1 point particularly to that as an area where the Government needs to be far more active. There are a variety of areas in which such construction will be needed. There are the inland fleets, particularly on the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes.
September 17, 1985

Offshore we have the fishing fleets and offshore drilling and supply, all of which is work that should be carried on by vessels constructed in Canada. Beyond that there is the larger question of whether or not Canadians should begin again the development of a deepsea shipping fleet. Having those vessels built in Canada would mean more work for our shipyards.
Now, I do not think I need to make arguments this afternoon about the economic value of such a program as one contemplates the decline in Government revenues which has been experienced and the cost of such programs as unemployment insurance. We have to consider carefully the way in which employment has fallen off in shipbuilding over the past 10 years, so one can appreciate the economic necessity for these things. However, I do not think I need to make those arguments at any length in the very few moments that I have because the Progressive Conservative Party in years past has recognized that.
The 1979 program of the Party called for the gradual development of a Canadian deepsea fleet. It called for the development of tax policies to permit pre-tax dollars to be spent on vessel replacement and to make available low interest loans to Canadian shipbuilders. It called for the restriction of Canadian waters, after 1985, north of 60, to Canadian designed and constructed vessels for all extraction and shipment of Canada's Arctic resources. On several other points they clearly recognize the needs of the industry. In 1984, the Party program again called for a number of actions designed to create a prosperous industry.
The shocking and quite incredible fact is that on this day, one year after the Government was sworn in, with a fiscal and economic statement delivered and a Budget passed, there has not been any action. It is not surprising that a Government Member was compelled to say to his constituents that the impact of the federal Budget on the shipbuilding industry in Canada was disastrous, to say the least. It is not surprising that the President of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Association should say that the P.C. record in recent years as far as shipbuilding goes is perfidious. These are incredibly strong words, but the sad fact is that the Liberals during the 1980s ran the industry towards disaster. However, a year has passed and there has yet been no clear cut plan laid out and no evidence that this Conservative Government intends to change direction and move the industry towards the viability and prosperity that it promised the people of Canada last summer.

Mr. Speaker, I would like in the first place to comment on the Hon. Member's contributions on the subject of a policy on changes in Canadian shipyards. To take up his question, yes, there is a study underway, as the Minister stated in the House last Spring, a study of the overall question, and as soon as there are discussions to be had with members in this House and announcements to be made, I am sure the Minister of Regional Indus-
Adjournment Debate
trial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) will be pleased to so advise the House.
However, I would like to comment on the example put forth by the Hon. Member to introduce his question, namely the Halifax shipyards.
I would like to remind him of what happened under this special project. On September 12, the Minister of Development for Nova Scotia announced that a group of prominent Halifax businessmen had purchased HIL. The consortium, led by a former President of St. John's Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Ltd. will take over management of HIL as of October 1985 and will become its owners as of January 1, 1986. The consortium will assume the provincial government's liability and invest an additional $1 million in capital.
Through various industry assistance programs the federal Government has injected some $49.6 million into the company since 1980. In addition, the contracts related to the three Coast Guard vessels currently being worked on at HIL have been renegotiated to permit the yard to complete this work. The three existing federal Government contracts will be completed at HIL, thereby providing continuing employment at approximately current levels for some months.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-WESTERN DROUGHT-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE. (B) REQUEST FOR DIRECT PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
AGRICULTURE-WESTERN DROUGHT-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE. (B) REQUEST FOR DIRECT PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 10, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) when he was going to make financial assistance available to the farmers in western Canada who have lost so much through the drought this year. For the last couple of weeks we have been debating a billion dollar disaster caused by this Government in the Canadian Commercial Bank. However, Mr. Speaker, there is an even bigger disaster in western Canada, the drought which has affected millions of acres of land at an estimated cost of $3 billion. In Saskatchewan alone over 30,000 farms were affected by this drought. Over 14 million acres of farmland have been devastated.
After prodding by the provincial government, the federal Government moved to provide assistance to the livestock industry, but it is still procrastinating on a decision with regard to the grain sector. The situation is desperate. There have been many meetings at which hundreds and hundreds of people have pleaded with the federal Government to take action. Fourteen hundred people attended a meeting in Ben-gough; 200 farm women attended another meeting there. At a meeting in Swift Current 500 people petitioned the Premier of Saskatchewan who was unwilling to meet the people who are facing this disaster. Other meetings were held in Ponteix, Kayville, and Climax where people called upon the Government for action. However, there is no action forthcoming.
This is a disaster of biblical proportions, Mr. Speaker, and the Government should be moving on it. Instead, we see

The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is calling for action. They have identified this as one of the most serious climatic disasters in the history of the province and are calling on the Government to provide a massive $500 million dollar drought aid package.

With respect to assistance for livestock producers, the province announced a program, saying that it would go to Ottawa to obtain more assistance. The federal Government, with a flourish, announced its program and indicated that the one program was supplementary to the other. In fact, the province grabbed the federal assistance so that the individual livestock producers ended up with nothing more than the provincial help. The Government should act soon and I hope that whatever form that assistance takes it will make the payment directly to the farmer so that the viability of this industry can be preserved. It is a matter of national urgency.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-WESTERN DROUGHT-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE. (B) REQUEST FOR DIRECT PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question put by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). I am sure he knows that we have spent the summer attending many meetings in the areas he has mentioned which have been devastated by drought. I want to assure him and the House that the Government has taken this issue very seriously.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) went to the Prairies and met the farmers in several areas, along with the Agriculture Ministers of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Subsequent to
that meeting, the Government responded quickly with respect to livestock in Phase 1 of the task force report. This amounted to some $48 million to the farmers to maintain their livestock herds.
The Hon. Member specifically mentioned the cost-sharing arrangement. He certainly should know that the arrangements between the province and the federal Government was cost sharing and the federal Government's commitment was $30 per head to the livestock producers. He must also understand that these agreements must be with all of the provinces on a fair basis and on a cost sharing arrangement.
With regard to Phase 2, any special assistance will be in addition to the crop insurance payments to Prairie producers, which are expected to total $500 million this year. The committee is now hard at work reviewing assistance requirements for crop damage. The full damage has not yet been assessed and, of course, it cannot be fully assessed until the crops are in. It would be irresponsible of the Government to prematurely put in place an assistance program for crop damage that may or may not be adequate to respond to the need. However, I can assure this House, on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture, that the committee will be in a position to make suggestions to the Minister just as soon as all the facts are on the table. I can also give the assurance that this Government will act quickly and responsibly once those recommendations have been received.
I also want to assure this House and the farmers of western Canada that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has been very concerned and asked me to report on a daily basis to him as to the seriousness of the drought. I am sure the farmers are very thankful for the type of consideration that has been given by this Government. I know in speaking to many of the livestock producers that they have been very pleased with the response which this Government has given.
